papers.title: Quasiparticle-induced transitions in a fluxonium qubit
papers.abstract: Quasiparticles are a prominent decoherence source in superconducting qubits, but their effects are notoriously difficult to isolate in fluxonium. Unlike the transmon, fluxonium is insensitive to offset charge, precluding charge-parity detection of quasiparticle tunneling. We address this challenge by measuring the excitation and de-excitation rates in a fluxonium qubit under controlled on-chip quasiparticle injection and isolating the quasiparticle-induced contribution by subtracting the background transition rates. We show that to accurately model the external magnetic flux dependence of the quasiparticle-induced transition rates, it is necessary to account for the superconducting gap asymmetry across the Josephson junctions. A comparison between theory and experiment constrains the relative quasiparticle densities in the small junction and the junction array and helps explain previously reported discrepancies between the bounds on the quasiparticle densities inferred for these two circuit elements.

summary.summary: This work measures quasiparticle-induced transition rates in fluxonium qubits under controlled on-chip injection and demonstrates that superconducting gap asymmetry $\delta\Delta/h \approx 1.72$ GHz across Josephson junction leads is essential for explaining the external flux dependence of these rates. The results show that accounting for $\delta\Delta$ resolves previously reported discrepancies between quasiparticle density bounds in the small junction versus the junction array, yielding consistent $x_{\mathrm{qp}} \approx 3 \times 10^{-6}$ across both elements.
summary.motivation: Quasiparticles are a major decoherence source in superconducting qubits, but their effects are difficult to isolate in fluxonium due to charge insensitivity that precludes charge-parity detection. Prior studies have reported puzzling discrepancies: bounds on $x_{\mathrm{qp}}^{\mathrm{small}}$ typically exceed $x_{\mathrm{qp}}^{\mathrm{array}}$ by orders of magnitude, but the origin of this disparity remained unclear.
summary.method: The authors performed controlled QP injection via a voltage-biased junction and measured quasi-instantaneous excitation and de-excitation rates $\Gamma_{\uparrow,\downarrow}$ at flux bias points ranging from integer flux quantum (IFQ, $\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}=0$) to half-integer flux quantum (HFQ, $\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}=0.5\Phi_0$). Background-subtracted QP-induced rates $\Delta\Gamma_{\downarrow,\uparrow} = \Gamma^{\mathrm{inj}} - \Gamma^{\mathrm{bg}}$ were modeled with $\delta E_{\mathrm{qp}} \sim \hbar\omega_{01} \sim k_B T_{\mathrm{qp}}/h \approx 1.2$ GHz and $\delta\Delta \neq 0$, independently measured from the resonant peak in $\Gamma_{02}$ at $\hbar\omega_{02} \approx \delta\Delta$.
summary.result: For qubit Q1 ($E_J/h=2.043$ GHz, $E_L/h=0.078$ GHz), one-parameter fits to $\Delta\Gamma_{\downarrow}$ assuming equal QP densities $x_{\mathrm{qp}}^{\mathrm{small}}=x_{\mathrm{qp}}^{\mathrm{array}}$ yielded $x_{\mathrm{qp}}=3.6 \times 10^{-6}$, consistent with the independent transmon measurement $x_{\mathrm{qp}}^{\mathrm{tr}}=3.0 \times 10^{-6}$. The two-peak structure in $\Delta\Gamma_{\downarrow}(\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}})$ with comparable magnitudes at IFQ and HFQ—inconsistent with prior models assuming $\delta\Delta=0$—is explained by suppression near HFQ via the condition $\delta E_{\mathrm{qp}} \lesssim \delta\Delta - \hbar\omega_{01}$.

papers.title: Component-Level Inverse Design of Transmon Qubits Using Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Designing a superconducting qubit to realize specific Hamiltonian parameters typically requires iterating through a time and compute-intensive forward loop in which the designer chooses a layout geometry, simulates it, extracts circuit parameters such as capacitances, and refines the geometry. We study the inverse version of this task using a neural-network workflow that maps target Hamiltonian parameters directly to component-level layout parameters, which we subsequently demonstrate on a planar transmon layout. During training, we pair the inverse model with a frozen forward surrogate model and evaluate the loss in Hamiltonian space rather than in layout-parameter space. In validation against a conventional EM solver, 97% of generated designs produce usable geometries, and the inverse-plus-surrogate pipeline reaches mean percent errors of 0.73% for qubit frequency and 1.58% for anharmonicity, comparable to or below the fabrication and simulation-to-measurement uncertainty expected for academic-process transmon devices of this type. A single pipeline query takes ~60 ms on CPU, versus ~2 min for a conventional EM capacitance extraction on the same hardware, a speedup of approximately 2,000x. Batching minimizes the AI model inference overhead, reducing the runtime to 3.1 microseconds per sample on CPU and 2.6 microseconds per sample on GPU at a batch size of 2048, resulting in speedups of 3.9 x 10^7 and 4.6 x 10^7, respectively, relative to a single conventional CPU EM extraction. Our results indicate that component-level inverse design usefully extends and complements conventional EM simulation, including for small datasets on the order of 1,000 samples.

summary.summary: This work demonstrates an inverse-design workflow for superconducting transmon qubits that maps target Hamiltonian parameters ($f_q$ and $\alpha$) directly to component-level layout parameters via a neural network paired with a frozen forward surrogate. Validation against conventional EM simulation achieves mean percent errors of 0.73% for qubit frequency and 1.58% for anharmonicity on 97 geometrically usable designs, with speedups of $3.9 \times 10^7$ on CPU and $4.6 \times 10^7$ on GPU at batch size 2048 relative to single EM extractions.
summary.motivation: Designing superconducting qubits currently requires iterative forward-loop simulation with expensive EM solvers, creating a bottleneck in QPU design. Direct mapping from target Hamiltonian parameters to physical geometry would accelerate candidate generation and enable systematic exploration of design space.
summary.method: An inverse MLP with one hidden layer (64 units, 387 parameters) was trained using a frozen forward-surrogate MLP (736 units, 4418 parameters) to enforce loss in Hamiltonian space rather than geometry space, addressing the ill-posed one-to-many nature of the inverse problem. Training used $\sim$1,000 samples from the SQuADDS cross-claw transmon dataset with min-max scaling and mean absolute error loss on scaled Hamiltonian parameters.
summary.result: On 97 valid EM-validated designs from held-out SQuADDS test records, the pipeline achieves median errors of 0.53% ($f_q$) and 1.14% ($\alpha$), comparable to combined simulation-to-measurement uncertainty for academic transmon processes. Single-sample inference takes $\sim$60 ms on CPU versus $\sim$2 min for conventional EM extraction; batched inference reaches 3.1 µs per sample on CPU and 2.6 µs on GPU, enabling rapid screening of candidate designs.

papers.title: Floquet Reservoir Engineering for Remote Logical Entanglement
papers.abstract: Implementing controlled dissipative dynamics is a powerful approach for state preparation in a variety of contexts, including the preparation of remote entangled states. Here, we show that by going beyond the standard setting of time-independent dissipative dynamics, one can realize even more powerful non-unitary protocols. We introduce dissipative Floquet protocols for stabilizing remote entanglement of logical qubits, where continuously-running dissipation is interleaved with a periodic sequence of unitary gates. These protocols harness existing experimental capabilities, and overcome time-entanglement limits that constrain standard approaches. They also implement an autonomous form of entanglement distillation. We show how these protocols give enhanced protection against waveguide loss, and as an example, analyze a specific implementation using cat-qubits and transmons in a superconducting circuit.

similar_to.title: Driven-dissipative entanglement of distant giant atoms
The Kerr-Cat Qubit: Stabilization, Readout, and Gates

summary.summary: This work introduces dissipative Floquet protocols that stabilize remote entanglement between logical qubits by interleaving continuous engineered dissipation on communication qubits with periodic unitary gates. The protocol overcomes the time-entanglement tradeoff of standard dissipative approaches and achieves autonomous entanglement distillation, with a concrete implementation using cat qubits and transmons in superconducting circuits.
summary.motivation: Standard time-independent reservoir engineering for remote entanglement suffers from fundamental limitations: most protocols cannot generate maximally-entangled states between remote qubits due to a time-entanglement tradeoff, and they cannot directly stabilize entanglement of protected logical qubits that do not couple to the engineered bath.
summary.method: The protocol uses two remote nodes, each with a logical qubit and a communication qubit coupled to a common dissipative waveguide or transmission line. Periodic control sequences interleave fast local CNOT and CZ gates between communication and logical qubits with continuous dissipation, creating a time-periodic non-unitary dynamics that autonomously mimics parity measurement and feedback without explicit measurements or classical communication. Analysis is performed for two entangling reservoirs: distributed two-mode squeezing and Rabi-driven chiral coupling.
summary.result: The protocol deterministically stabilizes maximally-entangled logical Bell states with convergence rate $\Gamma = -\ln(1-p_\mathrm{conv})$ depending on a detection probability $p_\mathrm{conv}$ extractable analytically for the two-mode squeezing scheme. Against waveguide loss $\epsilon$, the logical concurrence error scales as $1-\mathcal{C} \propto \epsilon$ (linear), substantially outperforming bare communication-qubit stabilization which scales as $\propto \epsilon^{1/2}$. For a cat-qubit implementation with $\gamma/2\pi = 10$ MHz, $\epsilon = 10^{-2}$, transmon $T_1 = 50$ µs, and cavity dephasing $T_{1,c} = 200$ µs, the protocol reaches steady-state concurrence $\approx 0.9$ with optimal stabilization time $\gamma\tau_\mathrm{stb} \approx 20$.

papers.title: Strategic Plan for Neutral Atom Quantum Computation
papers.abstract: We present a strategic plan for neutral atom quantum computation, bringing together hardware development and theory advancements to achieve the goal of practical quantum advantage. The concept of practical quantum advantage is defined, along with how to verify claims of advantage, and approaches to designing quantum algorithms that deliver practical advantage. Future directions for neutral atom quantum processor hardware are described: scaling-up system size, Qubit encodings and atomic platforms, going further below threshold with neutral-atom logical-qubit performance, continuous reloading of qubits, and fast readout. We also explore opportunities for scalable integrated photonic control technologies. Alongside hardware advancements, new developments in quantum error correction and compilation of quantum circuits are proposed. Finally, we examine the opportunity of networking multiple neutral atom quantum processors together to perform distributed quantum computing and overcome possible limitations of a single system.

similar_to.title: Fault-tolerant interfaces for modular quantum computing on diverse qubit platforms
Developments in superconducting erasure qubits for hardware-efficient quantum error correction

summary.summary: This strategic plan outlines a comprehensive roadmap for scaling neutral atom quantum computers from current thousands of qubits toward 10,000–100,000 physical qubits required for practical quantum advantage, integrating advances in hardware, photonic control, error correction, and circuit compilation. The plan emphasizes that neutral atoms have demonstrated below-threshold error correction, two-qubit gate fidelities exceeding 99.5%, and dynamically reconfigurable connectivity, positioning the platform to achieve megaquop-scale computations within the next decade.
summary.motivation: Neutral atom arrays have matured significantly, recently achieving the first below-threshold error correction demonstration with gate fidelities above 99.5%, making practical quantum advantage attainable. However, substantial challenges remain in scaling system size, controlling increasing numbers of qubits, and reducing cycle times for error correction, requiring coordinated theoretical and experimental advances.
summary.method: The plan identifies research directions across seven major areas: (1) defining and verifying practical quantum advantage with 10³–10¹² quops, (2) scaling qubit arrays to 10,000–100,000 atoms via higher laser power and optical lattices, (3) developing scalable integrated photonic control with silicon nitride and lithium niobate platforms, (4) implementing quantum error correction with high-rate qLDPC codes and improved decoders, (5) optimizing quantum circuit compilation for reconfigurable architectures, and (6) networking multiple QPUs through cavity-enhanced atom-photon entanglement and transportable arrays.
summary.result: Physical qubit counts have grown at ~1.8× per year while gate errors decreased by ~0.6× per year; recent demonstrations achieved distance-5 surface codes operating >2× below threshold with atom-loss detection. At current scaling rates, neutral atoms could reach utility-scale computation within the next decade, though this depends critically on closing the gap between current demonstrations (hundreds of logical qubits, MHz-level clock cycles) and practical requirements (>10⁶ quops, microsecond-scale readout).
